The session begins.

The Trade Way ends here in a press of wagons, mules and tired people. Ahead, the Basilisk Gate swallows the crowd a few at a time while soldiers of the Flaming Fist in red tabards look over every face. A broad-shouldered sergeant with a slate under her arm asks each traveller the same flat questions: name, business, where you'll sleep. Some she waves through. Some she sends to wait by the wall. Your cat walks along the edge of the cart ruts, tail high, and stops to sniff at something in the gutter. A skinny boy works his way down the line. "Bed, hot supper, honest prices, I know every inn in the Lower City!" Just off the road, under the first lamp to be lit, a woman in a patched green coat shuffles a deck with quick, easy hands. "One hand before the gate, friend? Luck favours the bold," she calls, and her eyes settle on you for a moment longer than on anyone else. The queue shuffles forward. Two more travellers stand between you and the sergeant, and the sun is going down behind the harbour.

The cards keep whispering behind you, a soft riffle and snap, like rain starting on a roof. Then they stop.

"An understanding," the woman in the green coat says. She doesn't sound offended. She squares the deck against the crate with one tap of her palm and looks at your hand on the pack strap, then up at your face. "Fair enough. Most people who say no just walk faster." She smiles a little, tired around the eyes. "Dessa. I'm here most evenings, if it ever stops being an understanding and turns into a habit."

She turns back to the road and calls the same offer to a drover behind you, without much hope in her voice.

Your thought reaches the cat as easily as reaching for your own pocket. Its answer comes back the way it always does, flat and unhurried, with a faint smell of wet stone in it.

*Not supper. A rat was here this morning. Old, sick, gone now.* A pause. In the gutter the cat stretches out a paw and doesn't quite touch whatever is there. *There's a copper down in the crack between two stones. Standing on its edge, and nothing is holding it up.* Another pause, longer. *I don't like it. Coins fall over.*

From where you stand you can just make out a dull disc of metal upright in the seam of the cobbles, catching the new lamplight on its rim. It might be wedged there. It might not.

The queue moves. Ahead of you, Sergeant Marsk looks at a tiefling man with two small children holding his coat. She marks her slate and points at the wall without a word. The man opens his mouth, shuts it again, and goes to stand with the others. Now only a heavyset wool merchant stands between you and the red tabard, and he is already digging through his satchel for papers.

The skinny boy has worked his way back down the line and is three people off, still shouting about honest prices, and he is looking at your cat.

Up close it's a common Baldurian copper, dull brown, its rim worn smooth by years of hands. It stands in the seam between two cobbles with the lamplight running along its top edge.

You give it time, the way the scouts taught you to look at a trail: one piece at a time, and nothing assumed.

Nothing is holding it up. The seam is a finger wide, wider than the coin is thick, and there is clear air on both sides of it. There's no grit packed under the rim, no wax, no bent nail, no wire. The copper stands on its edge on the bare stone at the bottom of the crack, perfectly upright, not leaning at all.

Then you see the second thing, and it's worse. The gutter runs downhill toward the harbour, and the day's runoff has left a grey tidemark of scum along the stones, full of straw and dung and a draggled feather. Where that line reaches the coin it bends. The scum curves around the copper in a neat, narrow loop and closes again behind it, the way water parts around a stone in a stream. Whatever came down this gutter today went around the coin and never knocked it over.

The face toward you shows Balduran's ship, the ordinary city stamp. Low on the rim there's a single bright nick where the wear has been scraped back to fresh metal, as though someone once tried to pry it loose.

You know something about coins like this, the way any man who has prayed to Tymora with a coin in his fist does. Her faithful flip coins for everything. In the temples down south they'd say a coin that lands on its edge isn't luck either way. It's a question the Lady hasn't called yet. Old soldiers made a joke of it. Nobody ever told you a coin could stay standing.

*It's been here longer than the rat,* the cat says. It smells of cold iron, like a key left out overnight. *All day, maybe. Nobody walks near it. Look at their feet.*

It's true. The queue's boots have worn a muddy track along the gutter's edge, and that track swings a little wide right here. Not by much, a hand's width. Nobody seems to know they're doing it.

"Oi, mister, mister. That your cat?"

The skinny boy drops into a crouch on your other side, quick as a sparrow. He doesn't look at the coin at all. Up close he's eleven at most, with a chalky smudge on one cheek, a jacket two sizes too big and very sharp eyes.

"Most inns in the Lower City won't take cats. Rats, they say, but they mean fleas." He talks fast, as if words are paid by the dozen. "But I know one that does. The Gilded Whisker, down Fishgut Lane, near the Mermaid. Cats sleep free, there's a dish of cream every night, the landlady's got four of her own. Two coppers and I'll walk you there. Honest price." He grins, showing a gap in his teeth. "What's his name?"

Behind you, the wool merchant has found his papers at last. Sergeant Marsk is reading them by lamplight, and in a moment she'll be calling for whoever's next.

The boy laughs, quick and surprised. "Cats never tell you nothing. My nan's cat lived fourteen years and never said a word to her, and she fed it every day."

The cat turns its head and looks at him. It doesn't blink. It keeps looking, steady and yellow-eyed, the way it looks at a man who has just said something not quite true. After a moment Pip blinks, rubs his nose with the back of his wrist, and turns to you instead.

"Pip. Pip Tallow. Tallow like candles, not like mutton." He doesn't follow your finger down to the copper. He keeps his eyes on your face, and his voice drops below the noise of the queue for the first time. "Noticed it? Everyone's noticed it. Nobody says so. It was standing there at sunup when I came through. Ferret had a go at it round noon, for a dare. He's a lad off the Rivington ferry. Bent nail, right there under the edge." He nods at the bright nick on the rim without looking at it. "The nail slipped and went in under his thumbnail, all the way up. Then his mam's washing line came down in the mud the same afternoon and he got a clouting for that too." He shrugs, and the big jacket shrugs a moment after him. "So I don't touch it. You shouldn't either, mister. Not with a cat that nice."

Up the queue the wool merchant gets his papers back and moves off under the arch, still tucking them into his satchel.

"Next," Sergeant Marsk says. The drover with the mules steps up into the place you left. Marsk's eyes pass over him to you, crouched in the gutter with a boy and a cat beside you, and stay there.

"You. In the cape." She taps the slate with her stylus. "You in this line or not?"

 (Out of game: none of these needed a roll, because each was plain talk or a gesture with nothing uncertain riding on it, and all four were played in the last turn.)

1. **His name:** Pip answered: "Pip Tallow. Tallow like candles, not like mutton." The line "He hasn't told me his name yet" was about the cat. The cat didn't give one, and the story left that alone.
2. **Two coppers:** You said the inn was "business we can discuss." That was an opening, not a payment, so no coin changed hands. The deal is still open and Pip is waiting on it.
3. **Pointing at the copper:** Done, without touching it. Pip nodded at the nick you pointed out but wouldn't look at the coin itself.
4. **Has he noticed it:** Pip said everyone has noticed and nobody says so. It was standing there at sunup. Ferret pried at it with a bent nail around noon, the nail went in under his thumbnail, and later that day his mother's washing line came down in the mud.

The turn ended on Sergeant Marsk's question, "You in this line or not?", so the next move is yours.

The drover's business takes less than a minute. Marsk looks at his mules, then at his face, and asks her three questions. He answers with three grunts, and she waves him through with the stylus. The mules clop under the arch and their smell goes with them.

Then it's you. Up close she is older than she looked from down the line, fifty or near it, with a burn scar on the back of her slate hand and a face that has stopped expecting anything interesting. She hears you out without interrupting. At "Queen Zaranda" her eyes drop to your cloak, the old Tethyrian cut and the faded regimental piping at the collar. Something in her shoulders settles a fraction, the way one old soldier recognises another.

"Zaranda's lot." She writes on the slate. "Scouts or line?"

She doesn't wait for an answer. Her stylus is already moving.

"Lady's Hall is in the Upper City. That gate shuts at dark and the Watch won't open it for prayers. Go in the morning." She scratches another mark. "Lodging."

Then she stops, with the stylus still touching the slate.

"The Gilded Whisker." She says it slowly. Her eyes go past your hip to Pip, who has come up beside you with his hands in the pockets of the big jacket. "On Fishgut Lane, would that be, Tallow?"

Pip doesn't miss a beat. "It's new, Sergeant."

"Course it is." Marsk looks at him for one more breath, long enough that the boy finds something interesting on the toe of his boot. Then she rubs out whatever she had written with the side of her thumb and writes something else. You can't see it from where you stand. She doesn't say what it is.

Down the wall, the tiefling father is still standing with his children, and the smaller one has fallen asleep against his leg.

Behind you the cards start again, a soft riffle and snap. The cat sits on your boot. You feel its weight there, and nothing else from it, not even a smell.

Marsk tucks the slate under her arm and looks at you properly for the first time.

"You stepped out of my line to crouch in my gutter, Worgen. Next to that." She doesn't look down at the copper. She very carefully doesn't. "What were you looking at?"

Place: Basilisk Gate, Baldur's Gate · Time: Day 1 · evening

Marsk hears "line first, scouts after" and gives one short nod. She doesn't write that down. She listens to the rest with the stylus resting on the slate, and when you say *Tymora* it stops moving.

"Haven't touched it." It isn't a question. "Good. Don't."

For a moment she looks past you, up the road at the queue and the lamps coming on along the wall one after another. When she speaks again it's at your volume, not hers.

"Nobody reports a penny in a gutter, Worgen. They report what comes after." She marks something without looking down. "Cart threw a wheel on the ramp at midday. Woman went down on those steps an hour back and broke her wrist. It's a gate. Could be any day."

From the set of her mouth, she doesn't believe it could be any day.

"Not the first one, either." She says this to the slate. "Last spring one stood on the Rivington ferry stairs. Three days. Nobody would go near it. On the fourth day the bottom flight went into the river with a crowd on it. Two drowned." She rubs her thumb once along the slate's edge. "Some kid kicked that one in afterwards. Don't know if it fell first."

She looks up, and her face is flat again.

"That's not a report. Lodging." Her eyes shift to your hip. "Tallow."

Pip straightens like he's been pinched. "Sergeant."

"Somewhere with a roof that's really there. Two coppers. If I hear otherwise, you're off my queue." She tips the stylus toward the arch. "Through. Upper gate opens at dawn for your temple. Next."

The tiefling father by the wall looks up hopefully as she calls it. She isn't calling him. He looks down again.

You walk under the arch with Pip half a step ahead. The wool merchant's smell of lanolin still hangs in the stone passage. Past it, the Lower City drops away toward the harbour in a staircase of roofs, chimney smoke and the first lit windows, with masts black against the last of the sunset. The cat walks at your heel. Halfway through the passage its thought arrives, quiet as a paw on a floorboard.

*She looked at it once. When you said the Lady's name.* A pause. *Damp ashes. That's what fear smells like on her.*

Pip spins round to walk backwards in front of you, hands deep in the big jacket, and finally meets your eye.

"Right. Real ones." He counts them off on his fingers fast, as if he's had them ready all along. "The Elfsong. Dear, but clean, and there's the singing at night if you like that sort of thing. The Blushing Mermaid. Cheap, takes anyone, takes your purse too if you sleep heavy. Or Mother Brindle's on Coppercoil Street. Boarding house, six rooms, a bit of stew. She doesn't love cats, but she hates rats worse." He hesitates, then adds, "That one's true, mister. All three are."

Place: Lower City, Baldur's Gate · Time: Day 1 · evening

Just past the arch, the Lower City opens out under you. The street falls away in worn steps and switchbacks between tall, narrow houses with leaning upper floors. Shutters bang as people close them for the night. A lamplighter on a ladder swears at his wick, and somewhere below a tavern door opens and lets out a gust of fiddle music before it shuts again. The air smells of tar, frying fish and a lot of people.

Pip stops when you do. He nods fast at "actual door," like a man shaking on it, but he doesn't grin. Your second question gets a different look from him. He studies you sideways for a moment, the way he studied the cat.

"Another staircase," he repeats. He says it carefully, without his usual speed. "Most people say it was just a bad day at the gate. Cart wheels go. Old women slip." He rubs the chalk smudge on his cheek and spreads it wider. "You don't say that."

Then he gets going again, quick and practical.

"Real priests of hers don't sleep down here. They live up the hill, with the money. They come down for funerals and when the Fist hangs somebody. Everybody else just flips a coin and hopes." He points down the slope with his chin. "There's a niche, though. Coppercoil Street, three doors up from Brindle's, in the wall of the old chandler's shop that burned out. A little stone lady holding a coin. People leave coppers in her lap and nobody nicks them, not even round here." He pauses. "And there's Wren. She sweeps it out mornings and puts new candles in. She used to wear the blue up at the Hall, people say. Then she didn't. I don't know what she counts as now. She's not a liar, though, and she lives over the candle-shop on the same street."

He glances back at the arch once. Past it, in the gutter you can't see from here, the copper is still standing.

"It's on the way, anyhow. Niche first, then Brindle's door." He shoves his hands deeper into the big jacket. Then, quietly, the way he spoke in the queue: "Mister, you really think something's coming down?"

Pip walks backwards for three more steps, studying your face. Then he turns round and walks properly, and for a little while he doesn't say anything at all, which on him looks like hard work.

"Ferret won't need telling twice. Not with his thumb how it is." He kicks a cabbage stalk into the gutter. "The others, though. Half the Rivington lot think it's a laugh. Spit at it from a pace off, see who flinches." He thinks it over. "All right. No dares. I'll say a man of the Lady's said so. They'll listen to that before they'd listen to me."

He takes you down the hill by a way no stranger would find. There's a flight of steps between two tanneries that stinks worse than the gate, then an alley so narrow your cape brushes both walls, then a sudden drop onto a cobbled street that bends round like the inside of a shell. The lamps are fewer here and set further apart. Above the doors hang painted signs, a boot, a kettle, a pair of scissors. Somewhere a woman is calling a child in for the third time, and getting crosser each time.

"Coppercoil," Pip says.

Halfway along, the street passes a blackened shopfront with boards nailed over the windows and a soot stain climbing the brick above them like a tongue. Set into the wall beside the dead door is the niche. It holds a stone figure no taller than your forearm, a woman with a coin raised in one hand and her other hand open in her lap. Two stubby candles burn at her feet. Her lap is full of coppers, a dozen or more, and every one of them lies flat.

The cat stops in front of it for the space of one breath.

*Tallow. Old smoke. People's hands.* It moves on. *Nothing wrong here.*

The candle-shop is four doors further on. Its shutters are up for the night, but there's a low light behind them, and a brighter one in the window above, where somebody has left the casement open a crack to let out the heat. There's a rack of dipped tapers hanging in the doorway to dry, white and pale yellow, swaying a little in the draught off the harbour.

Pip doesn't knock on the shop door. He goes to the side of the house, where a stair runs up the outside wall, and calls up at the open casement in a voice that's only half his queue-shout.

"Wren! It's Pip. Got someone for you. Not trouble." A pause. "Not *that* kind."

The light upstairs shifts. The casement swings wide, and a woman leans out on her forearms and looks down at the two of you, and the cat. She's in her forties, with a long, plain face and dark hair pulled back hard, going grey at one temple in a single clean streak. Her sleeves are pushed up and there's wax on her fingers. Round one wrist, where a bracelet might go, is a thin ribbon of faded blue.

She looks at Pip first, then at your cloak, then at the coin on its chain at your throat. She takes her time over that.

"He's seen the gate penny," Pip says up to her, quickly. "He says it's not a bad day."

Wren doesn't answer him. Her eyes stay on you, and her voice comes down low and even, pitched so it won't carry past the stair.

"Whose are you, sir? Did the Hall send you down here?"

Place: The candle-shop on Coppercoil Street · Time: Day 1 · evening

Wren lets a silence stand. Below her a taper on the drying rack knocks against its neighbour in the draught, a small hollow wooden sound.

"Marsk told you about the ferry stairs." She says it slowly, as if she's checking each word. "Hilde Marsk doesn't tell that to people. She tells them to move along."

She looks at Pip. Pip looks straight back at her, which seems to count for something, because she pulls her head in.

"Come up. Mind the fourth step, it's split. Pip, you wait at the bottom where I can see you, and don't touch my tapers."

"Wasn't going to," Pip says to the casement, which is already empty. He sits down on the lowest step with his elbows on his knees, settling in like he's done it before.

The outside stair is steep and worn hollow in the middle. The fourth step gives under your boot with a soft crack, and you put your weight on the edge. The cat goes up ahead of you without any trouble at all. A door at the top stands open on a single long room under the roof beams, hot as a bakehouse. A wax pot steams on a small iron stove, and the air is thick with the smell of tallow and beeswax and something sharper, like bay leaves. Dipped candles hang in pairs from a pole across the ceiling, so you have to duck your head between them. There's a narrow bed, a table scrubbed white, one chair, and on a shelf by the window a clay saucer holding a single coin, flat, beside a stub of blue candle that hasn't been lit.

The cat stops on the threshold and lifts its nose.

*Wax. Bay. A woman who sleeps badly.* A pause. *The saucer is old. Older than the room.*

Wren doesn't offer you the chair. She stands by the stove with her waxy hands loose at her sides, the blue ribbon dark against her wrist, and looks at you in the lamplight the way she looked from the window, only closer.

"I saw the one on the ferry stairs," she says. "Second step from the bottom, standing in a puddle that wouldn't touch it. I sat across the landing from it for two nights with a candle, so nobody would kick it for a laugh." Her mouth tightens. "Somebody kicked it anyway. After."

She doesn't say what she did on the third night, or whom she told. Her eyes go back to the coin at your throat.

"You say the Hall hasn't met you. Then they didn't give you that, and they didn't put you to her. So who did, sir?"

Wren hears you out without moving. The wax pot ticks on the stove. When you say *a card table* her eyes leave the coin at your throat, come up to your face and stay there for the rest of it.

"At a card table," she says. "Losing." She breathes out through her nose, close to a laugh but not quite one. "The Hall would like that less than you'd think, sir. They prefer people to come to her by the front steps, with an offering."

She hooks the one chair out from the table with her foot and turns it to face you. Then she sits down on the edge of the narrow bed herself, with her waxy hands on her knees.

"What they mean. I'll tell you what I was taught. They teach it to novices with a copper and a bare table. You toss it, it comes down ship or crown, and the Lady has answered. Once in a long while it lands on its edge, and the novice-mistress says the Lady is keeping her own counsel. A question not called yet. Then you pick it up and toss it again." Her hand goes to the blue ribbon at her wrist and stops there. "Nobody teaches what to do when you can't pick it up."

Above you a pair of candles turns slowly on the pole in the heat.

"Last spring I went up the hill about the ferry stairs. I asked for two priests to sit with the coin. I asked someone to look in the old day-books and see whether a coin had ever stood like that in this city before. They thanked me. They said the Hall's patrons did not need the Outer City's superstitions brought to their door." She waits a moment. "The stairs went on the fourth morning. I asked again after that, louder. That's all I'll say about the Hall tonight."

Then she answers your second question.

"The ferry coin stood three days, and it came on the fourth. The gate coin has been standing since sunup today. If it keeps the same count, and I don't know that it will, the bad thing comes three mornings from now. Maybe it won't wait that long. The ferry coin was in a puddle. This one's in the busiest gutter in the city."

“Luck and I have an understanding. No cards.”

Keeping my place in the queue, I reach out to the cat through our telepathic bond. *Found something worth the smell, or are you choosing supper?*

“James Worgen, late of Queen Zaranda’s army. Here to pay my respects at the Lady’s Hall and find work. Lodging isn’t settled yet—young Pip here recommends the Gilded Whisker.”

“Line first, scouts after. And I was looking at the copper, Sergeant. It’s standing on bare stone with nothing holding it upright. Even the gutter water’s gone around it.”

I keep my voice low enough not to carry down the queue.

“I serve Tymora. An edge-standing coin seemed worth a look—but I haven’t touched it. Has anyone reported trouble beyond the lad who tried to pry it loose?”

“Mother Brindle’s, then. You’ll get your two coppers when we reach her actual door.”

I stop just beyond the arch.

“But first: is there a shrine to Tymora down here, or one of her priests you know how to find? If that copper means another staircase coming down, I’d rather not spend the night waiting for the Upper City to open.”

“I don’t know, Pip. But there’s something wrong with that coin, and people have been hurt. That’s enough to ask for help.”

I nod down the street. “Take me to Wren first. And until we know more, no dares at that gutter—for you or your friends.”

“James Worgen. I serve Tymora, but the Hall hasn’t met me. I only reached the Gate this evening.”

I keep my voice as low as hers.

“The penny’s standing unsupported, and the runoff bends around it. Sergeant Marsk told me there was another at the ferry stairs before they collapsed. Pip thought you might know what we’re dealing with.”

I glance toward the stair. “May I come up?”

“She did. At a card table.”

I leave the coin resting against my chest.

“I’d staked everything and was losing. I prayed; she answered. Won the hand for me, then named her terms: no more cards, serve her, come to Baldur’s Gate. She said I’d learn what she needed here.”

I give a small, rueful shrug. “No introduction from the Hall, I’m afraid. Just a debt I intend to honour.”

“Do you know what the standing coins mean—and whether there’s still time to help the people at that gate?”

“Yes. I’ll ask for the old records in the morning, and come back with whatever I learn. James will do, by the way.”

I take the offered chair, careful of the hanging candles.

“Tonight I’d like to try a prayer beside the penny. No prying, no tossing it just to see what happens.”

I glance at the saucer. “Is that coin part of your devotions? I’d welcome some guidance before I try answering a question I haven’t heard.”

“I’ve carried out orders I didn’t like. Some were necessary. Some I should have questioned.”

I meet her eyes. “If it costs me comfort, coin, or a little blood, I’ll manage. If it means putting someone innocent in harm’s way, I’ll ask why. I owe her my service, not other people’s lives.”

I accept the taper carefully. “Thank you. Will you come with me? I could use someone watching my back who knows what we’re trying to do.”

“Brindle’s first. He’s earned his fee, not a place beside that penny.”

I head downstairs and address Pip without scolding him for listening.

“Come on, guide. Show me Mother Brindle’s door and I’ll settle up. Then home—not the gate. Find me here tomorrow if you want more honest work.”

“A room, please. James Worgen. I’ve business out tonight—how late can I return without waking the house?”

I offer her one gold piece. “Could you include two coppers in the change? I owe my guide.”

I count two coppers into Pip’s hand. “As agreed. Thank you, Pip. Tomorrow.”

The strongest part was the atmosphere. The standing copper was a good first mystery: small enough to investigate, wrong enough to worry about. The runoff bending around it and the unconscious detour of people’s feet made it memorable. The candle leaning against the wind was a satisfying payoff for choosing to act.

I liked the people. Marsk moving the lantern without acknowledging us said more than a speech would have. Wren had convictions and disappointments without immediately handing over her whole history. Pip gave James someone to treat decently. The cat’s sensory impressions were distinctive, useful, and often funny. James’s refusal to play cards also mattered without immediately forcing a temptation roll.

**What broke or dragged:**

- **The roll system did not use the sheet correctly.** Religion displayed “+4 Religion +3” and rolled +4; Persuasion displayed “+4 Persuasion +7” and also rolled +4. Those should have used +3 and +7 respectively. Neither changed the ultimate outcome here, but it undermines confidence in the mechanics. The journal also recorded the original Religion natural one rather than the accepted reroll.
- **The opening records contradicted campaign rules.** They assigned attunement slots to nonlegendary items despite the campaign’s explicit exception. Other differences between the supplied sheet and the opening records should have been briefly clarified rather than silently changed.
- **The unsolicited out-of-game explanations were distracting.** Several replies explained, at length, why my previous actions required no roll or that a promised morning visit had not happened yet. I hadn’t disputed either point. That felt like answering a complaint I never made.
- **Routine business took too many turns.** Getting an inn recommendation, obtaining change, paying Pip, and arranging lodging each received extensive treatment. Some of that established character nicely, but it crowded out adventure. By session’s end I had a compelling mystery, yet little actionable progress toward the crew-and-heist premise.
- Many NPCs shared the same cadence: pause, repeat my words, study me, deliver an oblique line. Individually effective; collectively noticeable.

**What I wanted more of:**

A clearer opportunity to make a consequential choice before the session ended. Receiving the card was exciting, but mostly supplied another mystery. One concrete lead—a named collector, an accessible record, a prospective crew member with a problem—would have given me something to pursue deliberately.

I’d also like the cat to offer clues without becoming the authority that interprets everything. Its claim that the flame was being *pulled*, rather than pointing, substantially supplied the interpretation after my failed check. Give me its strange impressions, but leave room for James to draw conclusions and be wrong.

Overall, I’d return. Keep the grounded NPCs, the unsettling details, and the respect for James’s choices. Tighten routine exchanges, fix the mechanical plumbing, and let the next session turn these excellent omens into a job I can start planning.

Yes—most clearly, I wanted to ask Marsk why the tiefling father and his children were being held.

They were repeatedly visible, and helping them fit James’s character. I held back because each exchange was already taking a full turn, while the coin seemed urgent. I worried that asking would open another lengthy conversation before I could act on the mystery. When Marsk finally let them through, I was relieved, but I’d missed the chance to choose whether to intervene.

I also wanted to challenge Dessa gently at the end. The cat suggested her story came suspiciously readily, and her proposed way to read the card went straight through James’s prohibition. I wanted to ask, “Who told you that story—and have you been waiting for someone carrying this card?” The session ended before I could pursue it.

The first was something I chose not to do because of pacing; the second was something I still wanted to do next.

I count two coppers into Pip’s hand. “As agreed. Thank you, Pip. Tomorrow.”

With a nod to Mother Brindle, I turn to join Wren and head back toward the Basilisk Gate.
turns.reply:
Pip holds his hand out flat, the way Mother Brindle counts change. You drop the coppers into it one at a time, and he closes his fist before the second one has stopped moving.

"As agreed," he says, trying it out, as if it's not a phrase he gets to use much. Then, quicker: "Tomorrow." He backs off the scrubbed step, gives the cat a small nod as if it outranks you, and goes off down Coppercoil Street at a trot, toward the harbour and away from the gate. He doesn't look back. He takes the corner by the scissors sign, and the big jacket disappears a moment after him.

Mother Brindle takes your nod with one of her own, about a finger's width. The door shuts. Behind it the chain doesn't go on. It's still well before midnight.

Wren falls in beside you without speaking. She takes the outside of the street, between you and the road, and the cat goes ahead of both of you, a pale shape between the lamps.

You go back the way Pip brought you: up the drop, through the alley where your cape brushes both walls, then the tannery steps, which smell no better in the dark. Halfway up, Wren talks without turning her head.

"There'll be three at the wall worth minding. A man in a leather apron who sits on the trough and sells nothing. Two brothers who stand by the horse post and argue so people stop to watch." She climbs another step. "The apron is the quick one. The brothers are there to make you look the other way."

*Tanner's lime. Old blood in the gutter-water,* the cat says from somewhere above you. A pause. *Something waiting at the top. Not people. Lamp oil, cold metal, the same as before.*

You come out under the wall a little after half past eight.

The queue has shrunk to a dozen people and a hand-cart, and the hurry has gone out of it. The lamps along the wall are all lit now, each in its own ring of light, and the dark between them is wide. The man in the leather apron is on the trough, exactly where Wren said he would be, picking at his teeth with a straw. Past him, by the horse post, two men with the same jaw are disagreeing loudly about a mule that isn't there. Neither of them looks at you. That is a kind of looking too.

The tiefling father is still by the wall. Both children are asleep against him now, one in his lap and one leaning on his shoulder, and he is sitting very straight so as not to wake them.

Dessa is still at her crate under the first lamp. Nobody is playing with her. She has a hand of patience laid out in rows on the crate and turns over a card now and then without much interest. She sees you come back. Her hand stops over the deck for a moment, then turns the next card.

Sergeant Marsk is still at the arch, with a lantern on a hook beside her and the slate under her arm. She looks at you, then at Wren in her plain dark coat, and her face doesn't change. She doesn't call you over. She reaches up, unhooks the lantern and hangs it again on the next hook along, two feet nearer the gutter. Then she goes back to the woman at the front of the queue.

The new light falls across the cobbles.

The copper is still standing in its seam, upright on bare stone, exactly as you left it. The scum line has dried grey around it in its neat closed loop. The boots of the evening queue have trodden a wide path round it, a little wider than before.

Wren stops one pace behind you and turns her back. You hear her shawl shift as she settles. Then her voice comes low over her shoulder, meant for you alone.

"I have the street, James. Whenever you're ready."

The cat sits down on the far side of the gutter, at the edge of the lantern-light. It looks at the coin and not at you, and it keeps its paws well clear.

turns.message:
I crouch beside the gutter and take out Wren’s taper. With a quiet word of Prestidigitation, I light its wick, holding it a hand’s breadth above the stone beside the copper.

I open my free hand, palm upward, without touching the coin.

“Lady Luck. I’m here, as you asked. I’m willing to be the one who catches it.”

I wait, watching the flame.
turns.reply:
You crouch at the edge of the gutter, where the lantern Marsk moved lights the cobbles. The taper comes out of your coat unbroken, still warm from your body and smelling sharply of bay. You murmur the cantrip under your breath. A spark jumps to the wick and catches, a small blue-hearted flame that steadies within a breath. You lower it until it hangs a hand's breadth above the bare stone, beside the copper but not over it. Then you turn your other hand palm up on your knee, open and empty.

"Lady Luck. I'm here, as you asked. I'm willing to be the one who catches it."

Behind you the queue murmurs along. One of the brothers at the horse post laughs at something. The cards at Dessa's crate stop.

At first the flame does what any flame does in the open. It wavers in the night air coming through the arch and bows a little toward the Outer City, the way the draught runs.

Then it straightens.

You don't see it happen so much as notice that it already has. The flame stands upright for the space of a heartbeat, perfectly still, as still as the copper beneath it. Then it leans the other way, slowly and deliberately, *into* the draught. It stretches long and thin and points away from the road and the Outer City. It points past the arch and up, over the roofs of the Lower City, toward the crown of the hill, where lamps glow behind the inner wall in the dark. It doesn't flicker. Wax runs down the taper onto your knuckles and you barely feel it.

Behind you Wren's shawl rustles. She has turned her head, only as far as she must, and you hear her breathe out.

"There," she says, almost too quietly to hear. Then the shawl rustles again as she turns back to the street.

You keep your hand open and try to read what you're seeing.

You've prayed to her in camp and on the road, and once over a losing hand. You never learned her rites in a temple, and nobody ever taught you to read a candle. You search your memory for anything a priest or an old soldier said about a flame that leans against the wind, and come up empty. You know what you're seeing. You don't know what it means: a direction, a summons, a warning, or only an answer to a question you never heard asked.

The flame keeps pointing uphill, patient as a compass needle.

The copper doesn't fall. It doesn't move at all. The only change is that the lantern light along its rim looks a little brighter where the flame leans over it.

The cat's thought arrives slowly, as if it has had to fetch it from far away.

*She heard.* A pause, long enough that you think it's finished. *It isn't pointing, James. It's being pulled. Like smoke going up a chimney.* Its whiskers flatten. *Cold up there. Old metal. Someone keeps a lot of it.*

It doesn't add anything else, and from the way it sits, it won't.

Behind you Wren's voice comes again, lower and quicker than before.

"The apron's off the trough. He's walking the long way round the queue toward us, slowly, with his hands in his pockets." She doesn't move. "The brothers have started on the mule again. Louder."

Wax runs warm over your knuckles. The flame keeps leaning toward the dark hill. Your palm is still open on your knee.

"She heard. But the cat says the flame isn't pointing. It's being pulled uphill, toward old metal."

Behind you Wren is quiet for a moment.

"Old metal," she says. "Up the hill." That's all. You hear her shawl settle as she turns her whole attention back to the street.

"Thank you, Lady," you murmur, and pinch the wick out. The flame doesn't fight you. It leans uphill to the last, and then there's only a thread of bay-scented smoke, and even that drifts up the hill and not with the wind. You stand. Your knees crack from crouching so long. The copper stays in its seam, upright and untouched, with the lantern light along its rim.

You turn round with your hands open in front of you.

The man in the leather apron is closer than you expected, perhaps three paces away. He has come round the end of the queue at an easy stroll, hands in his apron pocket and the straw still in his teeth. Up close he's about thirty, thin, with a broken nose and very clean hands for a man in an apron. He stops when you face him. He doesn't look caught. He looks like a man doing his sums over again.

Wren steps up beside you, on the side toward the street.

"Evening, Nettle," she says.

"Mistress Wren." He tips his head to her politely. Then he takes the straw out of his mouth and looks at you, at the dead taper, and last of all at the gutter. He doesn't let his eyes rest on the copper for long.

"Help me? No, friend." His voice is lazy and Lower City, with every word slow. "Thought I might help myself, to be honest. Man shuts his eyes by the gate after dark, that's what he's asking for. But you've gone and stood up." He shrugs, as if it's nobody's fault. "So I'll be neighbourly instead."

By the horse post the brothers have stopped arguing about the mule. Nobody watching would know when they stopped.

A thought arrives from the far side of the gutter, quiet and very flat.

*James.* A pause. *Your coat, left side, inside. There's something warm there that wasn't there when we came up the tannery steps.* Another pause. *Nobody's been near enough to put it there. Not him. Not anyone.* Its tail wraps tighter round its feet. *It smells like old lacquer. And a little like her.*

It doesn't say which "her" it means.

Nettle hasn't noticed any of this. He jerks his chin at the dead taper.

"Neat trick, that. Candle leaning against the wind, right at the gate's own bad penny. Half the queue saw it." He puts the straw back in his teeth and talks round it. "Thing is, friend, you're new, and there's people in this city who like to know when someone new sets up selling luck on their stones. Blessings, charms, a candle lit for a copper, whatever it is. They like to know first, and they like a cut." He rolls the straw to the other corner of his mouth. "So I'm asking, polite, before somebody less polite does. Who are you with?"

I leave my coat alone and meet Nettle’s eyes.

“James Worgen. I serve Tymora. No stall, no customers, no coin changing hands—just a prayer over something that’s already hurt people.”

I nod toward the gutter. “I’m not looking to start a business on anyone’s stones. I’m trying to keep those stones under our feet. If your people know anything about that penny, I’d welcome a word.”
turns.reply:
Nettle hears you out without moving. The straw stays still in his mouth the whole time, and his eyes go once to your open hands, once to the gutter, and back to your face.

Then he takes the straw out of his mouth and looks at it, as if it's the one that said something odd.

"Keep the stones under our feet," he repeats, slowly. "Huh."

He believes you. You can see it settle in him. The sums he was doing behind his eyes stop, and what's left is a thin man in an apron who's had a long evening and found nothing to show for it. He glances at Wren beside you, and that seems to finish it.

"Mistress Wren doesn't stand at the back of a man who sells candles for coppers. That's true enough." He puts the straw back. "So, a priest. Or near enough. I'll tell it that way, friend. The Lady's man, no stall, prays at bad pennies for nothing. Somebody'll want to know anyhow. They always do. But a priest gets left alone, mostly."

He looks at the gutter again, and this time he lets his eyes stay on the copper a moment longer than he likes.

"What my people know." He thinks about how much that's worth, and decides it's worth a little. "Old rule, downstairs. You don't work a street where one of those is standing. Purses go wrong, marks turn round at the wrong moment, a lad gets his hand stuck in a pocket. Nobody needs telling twice." He lowers his voice, though nobody's near. "And this spring somebody started paying for word of them. Silver, just to hear where one's stood and how long. Paid for the ferry one, after." He shrugs. "Who's paying, I couldn't say. Wouldn't if I could. But it wasn't us asking first. I know that much."

He steps back half a pace, as polite as he arrived.

"Evening, Mistress Wren. Friend." He nods at the cat, which is watching him without blinking. "And you."

He goes back the long way round the queue with his hands in his apron. When he passes the horse post he says nothing to the brothers, but a moment later they've drifted off together into the dark between two lamps, still arguing about the mule, and quietly.

Wren lets out a slow breath beside you.

"He'll tell them exactly what you said," she says. "Nettle doesn't lie downstairs. It's bad for business." She's still watching the place where the brothers went. "Someone paying silver to hear where the coins stand. That's new to me, James."

At the arch Marsk is waving a hand-cart through. She hasn't looked your way once. The lantern is still on the nearer hook.

On the far side of the gutter the cat hasn't moved. Its eyes have gone to your coat.

*Still warm,* it says. *Warmer, now he's gone.*

“Then someone may know more than the Hall admits. Another question for morning.”

I lower my voice. “The cat says something appeared inside my coat while we prayed. Warm, smells of old lacquer. Nobody put it there.”

Turning slightly to shield it from the queue, I carefully check my inside left pocket and show Wren what I find.
turns.reply:
"Morning," Wren agrees, and leaves it there.

You turn your shoulder to the queue. The lantern Marsk moved is behind you now, so your own body throws the shadow you need. You open the left side of your coat.

The taper is where you put it, against the pay slip. Below it, in the inside pocket where you've never kept anything but the odd coin, your fingers touch something smooth, flat and warm, like a stone that has sat all afternoon in the sun. You draw it out between two fingers, the way you'd take a card off the top of a deck. Your hand knows how to do that without being asked.

It is a card. It's a little narrower than a common playing card and thicker, cut from bone and lacquered until it shines like honey. The lacquer has crazed over the years into a fine web of cracks. The back is bare: no pattern and no maker's mark, only old ivory under the varnish.

The front has no suit and no number. In the middle of the card a single coin is painted, seen side-on, standing on its rim on a thin painted line of ground. Nothing holds it up. On one side of it a woman's face looks toward the coin, smiling, with her lips parted as if she's about to laugh. On the other side the same woman looks back at it, and she is scowling. The brushwork is fine and very old, and the colours have gone brown at the edges. The coin between the two faces stands dead level and leans toward neither of them.

You have handled a great many decks, Tethyrian, Amnian and Calishite, marked and honest, and some you only saw on other men's tables. You have never seen a card like this one, in any game. But any man who has prayed to Tymora on the road knows those two faces. The Lady has a sister, and every soldier who has rolled dice in a tent knows her name and doesn't say it near the dice.

Wren looks over your arm. She doesn't reach for the card. She looks at the painted coin for a long moment, then at the smiling face, then at the scowling one, and her mouth goes thin.

"That's no gate trinket," she says, very low. "That's bone, and the lacquer is older than I am. Older than Brindle." She keeps her eyes on the scowling face. "The Hall puts the Lady on its windows alone. Nobody I was ever taught by painted the two of them together like that, with something standing between them."

From the far side of the gutter, the cat's thought comes slowly.

*Old lacquer. Bone. A shut room somewhere a long way up.* A pause. *And her. Both of hers.* Its tail moves once across the cobbles. *It came when the flame leaned. Not before.*

Behind you a card snaps down on the crate under the first lamp. Then, for a moment, no more cards come.

The warmth of the card has spread into your fingertips. Your thumb has settled on its edge, where a man's thumb goes when he's deciding whether to play a card or keep it back.

Wren notices it too. Her eyes come up from the card to your face.

"You told me she took the cards away from you, James," she says. "So why would she put one back in your pocket?"

You ease your thumb off the edge. It takes more effort than it should. The card goes back into the inside left pocket of your coat, flat against the pay slip. Your own deck stays where it has been since the card table, at the bottom of your pack, and you leave it there. The warmth of the bone sits against your ribs like a hand.

Wren watches you put it away. "Good," she says, and nothing more.

When you mention Dessa she glances toward the crate under the first lamp. "She's had that spot a few months. Deals to anyone who'll sit. I've never heard of her being trouble." She pauses. "I've never heard of her winning much either."

You turn toward the crate and keep to the far side of the gutter, well clear of the copper. The cat crosses behind you, unhurried, and sits down a pace from the crate where the lamplight ends.

Dessa doesn't pretend she wasn't watching. She has stopped her game of patience. Her hands rest flat on top of the deck, one on the other, the way a dealer covers the cards when a hand is over.

"Did I see anything." She thinks about it properly before she answers. "The penny didn't do a thing, friend. I was looking right at it. Your candle did everything." She tips her chin up toward the dark crown of the hill. "Half the queue saw it lean, and the other half will have heard by morning."

Then she drops her voice, and her face looks tired again.

"I'll tell you why I stopped dealing, since you're asking straight. When the flame went over, my cards went cold. Not the night air. Cold like they'd been in a cellar." She turns her top hand over and looks at the palm, as if the cold might still be there. "Twelve years with a deck and that's never happened. So I put them down and watched you instead."

The cat looks at her the way it looks at most people, steady and yellow-eyed. Dessa looks back at it, and smiles a little, and doesn't blink.

*Orange peel,* it says. *Cheap ink. Old cards, a lot of hands on them.* A pause. *Nothing else. She's calm.*

"And nobody came near you while you knelt there," Dessa goes on, more briskly. "Not Nettle, not the brothers, nobody. I'd have seen. Watching hands is the only thing I'm any good at." She lets that settle, and then her eyes go once, very briefly, to the left side of your coat. "So when you stood up and pulled something out of there, I'll admit I wondered. You held it the way a man holds a card when he hasn't made up his mind whether to play it."

She doesn't reach for her deck. She keeps both hands on top of it, in plain view.

"What was it you found in your pocket?"

I keep it in my pocket.

“You’ve watched more tables than I have, I suspect. Ever seen a card like that, or heard of a deck it might belong to?”

Dessa listens without interrupting. When you say *a coin on its edge*, her eyes go to the gutter, then come back to you.

"Bone, under old lacquer," she says. "No suit." For a moment she looks at the patience laid out in rows on the crate as if it had disappointed her. "Never held one. I've heard of one, maybe. There's a story the sharps tell on the Chionthar barges, the old ones, when the wine's gone round twice. They call it the sisters' deck."

She gathers the patience into a pile while she talks, unhurried. Her fingers are quick and tidy, and she never really looks at what they're doing.

"Long ago some rich man up the hill had a deck painted, so he'd know which way his luck was leaning before he sat down to play. The painter went strange afterwards. The deck got broken up, and now and then a card turns up in the Undercellar and goes for more than a ship." She shrugs. "I always took it for a barge story. Every deck on the river is the devil's own deck by the end of the night."

Behind your shoulder, Wren speaks quietly.

"Which rich man?"

"The story never said, mistress. They don't." Dessa smiles at her, tired and friendly. Then she looks back at you, and her voice goes a little softer. "The old men said you read one by laying it down. Face up, on a table, with a hand dealt round it. The card shows you what the hand would have done." She tucks the squared deck into the inside of her green coat. "Not much use to a man with your understanding, I suppose."

The cat hasn't moved from its place at the edge of the lamplight.

*Orange peel,* it says. A pause. *She didn't have to look for that story. It was already there in her pocket.*

It says nothing more. Dessa gets up off her stool and stretches until her back clicks, and turns the crate on its side so it stops being a table.

"I'm done for the night, friend. Nobody plays after nine." She nods at Wren, and once at the cat, which doesn't nod back. "Most evenings. You know where."

note.text:
The strongest part was the atmosphere. The standing copper was a good first mystery: small enough to investigate, wrong enough to worry about. The runoff bending around it and the unconscious detour of people’s feet made it memorable. The candle leaning against the wind was a satisfying payoff for choosing to act.

I liked the people. Marsk moving the lantern without acknowledging us said more than a speech would have. Wren had convictions and disappointments without immediately handing over her whole history. Pip gave James someone to treat decently. The cat’s sensory impressions were distinctive, useful, and often funny. James’s refusal to play cards also mattered without immediately forcing a temptation roll.

**What broke or dragged:**

- **The roll system did not use the sheet correctly.** Religion displayed “+4 Religion +3” and rolled +4; Persuasion displayed “+4 Persuasion +7” and also rolled +4. Those should have used +3 and +7 respectively. Neither changed the ultimate outcome here, but it undermines confidence in the mechanics. The journal also recorded the original Religion natural one rather than the accepted reroll.
- **The opening records contradicted campaign rules.** They assigned attunement slots to nonlegendary items despite the campaign’s explicit exception. Other differences between the supplied sheet and the opening records should have been briefly clarified rather than silently changed.
- **The unsolicited out-of-game explanations were distracting.** Several replies explained, at length, why my previous actions required no roll or that a promised morning visit had not happened yet. I hadn’t disputed either point. That felt like answering a complaint I never made.
- **Routine business took too many turns.** Getting an inn recommendation, obtaining change, paying Pip, and arranging lodging each received extensive treatment. Some of that established character nicely, but it crowded out adventure. By session’s end I had a compelling mystery, yet little actionable progress toward the crew-and-heist premise.
- Many NPCs shared the same cadence: pause, repeat my words, study me, deliver an oblique line. Individually effective; collectively noticeable.

**What I wanted more of:**

A clearer opportunity to make a consequential choice before the session ended. Receiving the card was exciting, but mostly supplied another mystery. One concrete lead—a named collector, an accessible record, a prospective crew member with a problem—would have given me something to pursue deliberately.

I’d also like the cat to offer clues without becoming the authority that interprets everything. Its claim that the flame was being *pulled*, rather than pointing, substantially supplied the interpretation after my failed check. Give me its strange impressions, but leave room for James to draw conclusions and be wrong.

Overall, I’d return. Keep the grounded NPCs, the unsettling details, and the respect for James’s choices. Tighten routine exchanges, fix the mechanical plumbing, and let the next session turn these excellent omens into a job I can start planning.

after.text:
Yes—most clearly, I wanted to ask Marsk why the tiefling father and his children were being held.

They were repeatedly visible, and helping them fit James’s character. I held back because each exchange was already taking a full turn, while the coin seemed urgent. I worried that asking would open another lengthy conversation before I could act on the mystery. When Marsk finally let them through, I was relieved, but I’d missed the chance to choose whether to intervene.

I also wanted to challenge Dessa gently at the end. The cat suggested her story came suspiciously readily, and her proposed way to read the card went straight through James’s prohibition. I wanted to ask, “Who told you that story—and have you been waiting for someone carrying this card?” The session ended before I could pursue it.

The first was something I chose not to do because of pacing; the second was something I still wanted to do next.

opening.text: The Trade Way ends here in a press of wagons, mules and tired people. Ahead, the Basilisk Gate swallows the crowd a few at a time while soldiers of the Flaming Fist in red tabards look over every face. A broad-shouldered sergeant with a slate under her arm asks each traveller the same flat questions: name, business, where you'll sleep. Some she waves through. Some she sends to wait by the wall. Your cat walks along the edge of the cart ruts, tail high, and stops to sniff at something in the gutter. A skinny boy works his way down the line. "Bed, hot supper, honest prices, I know every inn in the Lower City!" Just off the road, under the first lamp to be lit, a woman in a patched green coat shuffles a deck with quick, easy hands. "One hand before the gate, friend? Luck favours the bold," she calls, and her eyes settle on you for a moment longer than on anyone else. The queue shuffles forward. Two more travellers stand between you and the sergeant, and the sun is going down behind the harbour.
